title: A New Heaven, a New Earth, and the Holy City
summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with humanity: he will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, and pain will be no more. An angel then shows John the city in detail, a vast cube of gold and precious stones with twelve gates and twelve foundations, with no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and with the glory of God as its light.
story: Everything in Revelation has been heading here, and so has everything in the Bible. The judgment of chapter 20 cleared away evil and death; now God does what he promised through Isaiah: “I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). The first creation began with “the heavens and the earth” in Genesis 1:1, and the Bible's story closes with a new heaven and a new earth. What was lost in Genesis 3, God's presence with his people, returns in fuller form than Eden ever had. The prostitute city of chapters 17 and 18 is replaced by the bride city. The garden has become a city, and the city is also a temple. The last chapter will add the river and the tree of life, completing the picture.
historical:
John's first readers were small congregations in cities of Asia Minor, some under pressure, some growing comfortable. They lived among great civic buildings, temples to the emperors, and the constant presence of Rome's wealth. Many of them would have known that Jerusalem and its temple had been destroyed by the Romans in AD 70 (if the book was written after that date, as most scholars hold). Against that background, a new Jerusalem coming down from God, one that no army could take and in which there was no temple building because God himself was present, was a promise of a very different future from the one Rome offered. The hope was not new with John: Isaiah, Ezekiel, and later Jewish writers all looked for a renewed and glorified Jerusalem, and Paul spoke of “the Jerusalem above” (Galatians 4:26).

The measurements are given in the units of the day. A stadion (plural stadia) was about 185 meters, so 12,000 stadia is roughly 2,200 kilometers or about 1,400 miles, a city far larger than any city on earth. A cubit was a forearm's length, about half a meter, making the wall 144 cubits (about 65 meters) thick or high. The text doesn't say which.
cultural:
The city's shape and materials come from Israel's worship. Its equal length, width, and height make it a cube, which recalls the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelt (1 Kings 6:20). The whole city has become the Most Holy Place. Its twelve foundation stones recall the twelve gems set on the high priest's breastpiece, each engraved with the name of a tribe (Exodus 28:17-21), though the ancient names of precious stones don't always match modern ones, so exact identifications are uncertain. The gates bearing the names of Israel's twelve tribes and the foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles show that the people of God, old covenant and new, form one city. Ezekiel's closing vision also has twelve gates named for the tribes (Ezekiel 48:30-35).

The covenant formula, “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (verse 3), echoes promises repeated through the Old Testament, such as Leviticus 26:12 and Ezekiel 37:27: “I will be their God, and they will be My people.” The word for dwelling place is the word for tent, recalling the tabernacle, the tent where God lived among Israel in the wilderness. The phrase that the sea was no more (verse 1) would have spoken in two ways: in the Old Testament and in Revelation the sea is often a symbol of chaos and the place from which the beast rose (Daniel 7:3; Revelation 13:1), and for John, exiled on the island of Patmos, it was also what separated him from the churches.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1-8 are an overview, climaxing in one of the rare places in Revelation where the One seated on the throne speaks directly: “Behold, I make all things new” and “It is done!” Verses 9-27 (continuing into 22:5) are a detailed tour of the city, introduced by one of the bowl angels with the same words used in 17:1 to introduce the prostitute. The parallel is deliberate. Babylon is a prostitute clothed in borrowed luxury and drunk on blood; Jerusalem is a bride adorned by God and shining with his glory. The chapter is dense with twelves and their multiples (twelve gates, twelve angels, twelve tribes, twelve foundations, twelve apostles, 12,000 stadia, 144 cubits), numbers that in Revelation belong to the people of God. It is poetry of a high order, and it is best read as a vision to be pondered rather than a blueprint.

outline.t: A new heaven and new earth, and God dwelling with his people
The One on the throne: I make all things new
The bride, the holy city, with its gates and foundations
The measuring of the city and its precious stones
No temple, no sun, no night: God and the Lamb are its light

doctrines.note: God does not abandon the world he made; he makes all things new. Christians differ on whether the new creation is the old one purified and renewed (often pointing to Romans 8:21) or a wholly fresh creation after the first passes away (often pointing to 2 Peter 3:10-13). Both confess a real, physical new creation, not a disembodied heaven.
The Christian hope is resurrection life in a renewed world where God himself will wipe away every tear. The promise is not that suffering was unreal but that it will be ended and answered.

The goal of the whole story is God with us: “the dwelling place of God is with man” (verse 3). The city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and the covenant promise reaches its fullest form.
The people of God, Israel's twelve tribes and the Lamb's twelve apostles, are one city and one bride, built by God and adorned for him.

words.note: Kainos, new. Greek had another common word for new in the sense of recent. Kainos often carries the sense of new in kind or quality, renewed and fresh. Many scholars think that shade matters here: the new creation is the world made new rather than simply a second, unrelated world, though the word alone can't settle the question.

Skene, tent or tabernacle, translated dwelling place in verse 3. It recalls the tabernacle of Exodus, where God's glory lived among Israel, and John 1:14, where the Word “made His dwelling among us,” using the related verb. What began in the wilderness tent and came in Jesus now reaches all creation.

Numphe, bride. The city is “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (verse 2) and called “the bride, the wife of the Lamb” (verse 9). The image joins the marriage of 19:7 with the city of chapter 21: the new Jerusalem is not mainly a place but a people united to God.

Naos, temple or sanctuary, the inner shrine where a deity was thought to dwell. John sees no naos in the city (verse 22), which is startling for a vision of Jerusalem. The reason is not that worship has ended but that God's presence now fills everything; there is no longer any need for a separate holy place.

christ: Christ is present throughout the city as the Lamb: the bride is “the wife of the Lamb” (verse 9), the apostles on the foundations are the Lamb's apostles, the Lamb is the temple together with God (verse 22) and is its lamp (verse 23), and the names of the citizens are written in “the Lamb's Book of Life” (verse 27). The title the Alpha and the Omega, spoken by God in verse 6, is spoken by Jesus in 22:13, so that the beginning and end of all things is identified with him. The promise that God will dwell with his people fulfills what began when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and Jesus' promise to prepare a place for his disciples (John 14:2-3) finds its answer here. The one who died and rose bodily is the firstfruits of this new creation; the renewed world is his resurrection extended to everything.

hard.q: Is the new Jerusalem a literal city, and what happens to this world?
hard.a:
Readers take the city in different ways. Some expect a literal city of the dimensions given, the capital of the new earth. Many others, noting that the dimensions, materials, and numbers are all symbolic (a cube like the Most Holy Place, twelves for the people of God, a street of gold as clear as glass), read the city as a picture of the people of God perfected and filled with his presence, since the city is also called the bride. Many hold elements of both: a real new creation, described in symbols that convey more than a map could.

On the fate of this world, Christians also differ. Some stress continuity: creation will be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:21), purified rather than annihilated, and even the glory and honor of the nations will be brought into the city (verse 26). Others stress discontinuity, noting that the first heaven and earth pass away (verse 1) and that 2 Peter 3 speaks of the elements dissolving. Most interpreters across traditions agree on the central point: the Christian hope is embodied, earthly in the renewed sense, and shared, not an escape of souls from matter.

questions: The Bible ends with God coming down to dwell with people, not people escaping to somewhere else. How does that change the way you think about heaven and about this world?
Verse 4 promises that God will wipe away every tear. What grief in your life or someone else's do you long to see answered this way?
The glory of the nations is brought into the city. What good work, culture, or beauty in this world might you hope to see redeemed rather than discarded?
